papers.title: Förtroendeingivande kommunikation i mötet med en social robot vid läkemedelsrådgivning på apotek
papers.abstract: Digitalisering och automatisering påverkar i allt högre grad hälso- och sjukvården, även inom apoteksverksamhet, där sociala robotar introduceras som stöd för information och rådgivning. Samtidigt väcker användningen av sådana tekniska lösningar frågor om hur kommunikationen upplevs när läkemedelsrådgivning inte sker i mötet med en människa. Kommunikation är central i vårdnära sammanhang och har betydelse för både trygghet, tillit och patientsäkerhet. Syftet med denna studie är att undersöka hur kunder upplever kommunikationen med en social robot i samband med läkemedelsrådgivning på apotek, med särskilt fokus på hur kommunikativa uttryck relaterar till förtroendet för rådgivningen. Studien tar sin teoretiska utgångspunkt i kommunikation som en interaktiv och relationell process samt i Jean Watsons Theory of Human Caring, som används som ett analytiskt ramverk för att belysa hur tillit och trygghet kan förstås i vårdande kommunikation, även i teknikmedierade möten. Studien har genomförts med en kvalitativ forskningsdesign. Datamaterialet består av semistrukturerade intervjuer med kunder som interagerat med en social läkemedelsrobot i apoteksmiljö. Materialet analyserades med kvalitativ innehållsanalys enligt Graneheim och Lundman, med fokus på att identifiera återkommande mönster i deltagarnas upplevelser. Resultaten visar att deltagarnas upplevelser av kommunikationen påverkades av flera samverkande faktorer, vilka organiserades i tre övergripande teman: visuella och emotionella intryck, språkliga egenskaper samt samtalsdynamik och kommunikativ klarhet. Robotens röst, språkbruk och samtalsstruktur hade stor betydelse för upplevelsen av tydlighet och professionalism, medan visuella uttryck såsom blick och ansiktsuttryck påverkade känslor av trygghet eller obehag. Vidare framkom att kommunikativ neutralitet och ett icke-dömande förhållningssätt i vissa situationer kunde upplevas som förtroendeingivande. Studien drar slutsatsen att sociala robotar kan fungera som ett komplement i läkemedelsrådgivning, men att kommunikativa egenskaper är avgörande för hur interaktionen upplevs. Resultaten understryker vikten av att beakta både verbala och icke-verbala aspekter av kommunikation vid utveckling och implementering av robotbaserade rådgivningslösningar i apoteksmiljö.

QP1.section: 8. Resultat > 1.3. Positiva visuella signaler i interaktionen
QP1.text: Trots förekomsten av obehagliga intryck var det även flera deltagare som lyfte fram att robotens blick kunde uppfattas som varm och vänlig. En deltagare berättade exempelvis: ”Han hade mysiga ögon… väldigt sådär vänliga” (T11), medan en annan beskrev att roboten gav ”en mjuk blick” (T57). Dessa mer positiva beskrivningar tyder på att visuella aspekter kan bidra till en känsla av social närhet och göra interaktionen mer tillgänglig, även om roboten inte uppfattas som fullt mänsklig. Ögonkontakt framstod som särskilt betydelsefull. För en deltagare fungerade robotens blick parallellt till ett gott kundbemötande: ”Den sökte dendär ögonkontakten… det gör ju en trevlig kundrådgivare också” (T33). Detta visar att visuella signaler inte bara påverkar hur mänsklig roboten upplevs, utan också hur professionell, lyssnande och engagerad den framstår. I dessa fall verkar robotens design och blickstyrning ha skapat en känsla av att bli ”sedd”, vilket kan vara en central faktor för att etablera förtroende även i en tekniskt förmedlad interaktion.

QP1.section: 9. Diskussion > 9.1. Blick och ansiktsuttryck som förtroendeskapande faktorer
QP1.text: Resultaten visar att robotens visuella uttryck, särskilt blick och ansiktsuttryck, hade stor betydelse för hur interaktionen med den sociala roboten upplevdes. Flera deltagare beskrev robotens blick som tom eller intensiv, vilket i vissa fall väckte obehag och påverkade känslan av trygghet negativt. Samtidigt framkom även mer positiva upplevelser där robotens blick uppfattades som vänlig och engagerad, vilket bidrog till en känsla av att bli sedd och bemött på ett professionellt sätt. Dessa resultat ligger i linje med tidigare forskning som visat att blickbeteende är en central social signal även i interaktion mellan människa och social robot (Babel m.fl., 2021; Okuda m.fl., 2025). Dessa studier har visat att robotens blick kan förstärka upplevelsen av social närvaro och engagemang, men att avvikande eller statiska blickmönster också kan upplevas som onaturliga och skapa obehag. Resultaten i denna studie bekräftar därmed att visuella signaler spelar en avgörande roll för hur mänsklig och tillitsfull roboten uppfattas, särskilt i rådgivningssituationer där trygghet är central. Resultaten kan vidare förstås i relation till att blickens betydelse är starkt situationsberoende. I likhet med Okunda m.fl. (2025) framträder att robotens blick inte per automatik upplevs som positiv, utan att dess effekt beror på hur väl den överensstämmer med användarens förväntningar och den aktuella kontexten. I en rådgivningssituation där ämnet kan upplevas som personligt eller känsligt kan en avvikande, statisk eller intensiv blick förstärka osäkerhet snarare än skapa social närvaro. Detta kan bidra till en minskad känsla av trygghet, även om den verbala informationen i sig skulle vara korrekt. Watson betonar att tillit och emotionell trygghet skapas genom upplevelsen av närvaro och uppmärksamhet i mötet (Watson & Leininger, 1985). När robotens visuella uttryck uppfattades som bristande eller avvikande kan detta tolkas som en begränsning i möjligheten att skapa en sådan relationell trygghet. Samtidigt visar de positiva beskrivningarna att även tekniska lösningar, genom visuella signaler som uppfattas som vänliga och lyhörda, kan bidra till en grundläggande känsla av förtroende i interaktionen.

QP1.section: 8. Resultat > Tema 1: Visuella och emotionella intryck
QP1.text: Detta tema beskriver hur robotens visuella uttryck och emotionella intryck påverkade deltagarnas upplevelse av trygghet, obehag och engagemang i kommunikationen.

QP2.section: 8. Resultat > 1.3. Positiva visuella signaler i interaktionen > Tema 2: Språkliga egenskaper
QP2.text: Detta tema beskriver hur robotens språkliga egenskaper, såsom röst, språkbruk och språklig anpassning, påverkade deltagarnas upplevelse av tydlighet, förståelse och förtroende i kommunikationen.

QP2.section: 8. Resultat > 2.1. Rösten som bidragande faktor till trygg kommunikation
QP2.text: Deltagarna beskrev ofta robotens röst som tydlig, lugn och professionell, vilket bidrog till en grundläggande känsla av trygghet och förutsägbarhet i kommunikationen: ”Den var behaglig tycker jag… såhär mänsklig” (T13). Samtidigt kunde andra uppleva rösten som onaturlig, repetitiv eller monotont framförd. En deltagare uttryckte att roboten hade en ”behaglig röst, men inte så naturlig” (T5), medan en annan beskrev sättet att tala som ”väldigt monologt… töt- töt-töt” (T33). Detta illustrerar att även om rösten uppfattas som funktionell, kan bristen på variation i tonfall skapa en känsla av distans i interaktionen. Flera deltagare kopplade robotens röst till andra välkända digitala assistenter, vilket visar att rösten tolkades inom ramen för tidigare erfarenheter av teknologi. Som en deltagare uttryckte det: ”det kändes som AI-röst… men inget problem” (T57). Rösten var för flera av deltagarna ändå som de förväntat sig “kändes inte helt naturligt den där melodin på rösten... man kanske förväntar sig lite att det ska vara så då det är en robot” (T5).

Analysen resulterade i tre teman som beskriver hur deltagarna upplevde kommunikationen med den sociala roboten vid läkemedelsrådgivning: (1) visuella och emotionella intryck, (2) språkliga egenskaper, samt (3) samtalsdynamik och kommunikativ klarhet. Nedan presenteras resultaten strukturerat i teman och subteman, med beskrivande citat som är skrivna med kursiv text. För att säkerställa deltagarnas anonymitet har citaten kodats med beteckningen T följt av ett nummer (t.ex. T1, T7, T53). Kodningen kommer från forskningsprojektets interna numrering och motsvarar inte ordningen i intervjuerna. Koderna kan inte kopplas till enskilda individer. Tabell 1. QP3.section: 8. Resultat > Tema 1: Visuella och emotionella intryck
QP3.text: Detta tema beskriver hur robotens visuella uttryck och emotionella intryck påverkade deltagarnas upplevelse av trygghet, obehag och engagemang i kommunikationen.

QP3.section: 8. Resultat > 1.1 Upplevelser av robotens bristande mänsklighet
QP3.text: Många deltagare upplevde robotens utseende och beteende som mindre mänskligt och delvis mekaniskt, vilket påverkade hur naturlig och trygg interaktionen kändes. En deltagare beskrev roboten som ”mer mekanisk” och jämförde interaktionen med en verklig människa: ”… man känner kanske inte att man får lika mycket empati av en robot” (T4). Detta visar att frånvaron av mänskliga uttryck och tydliga sociala signaler kan göra det svårare att uppleva närvaro och känslomässigt stöd. Flera deltagare uttryckte också att roboten framstod som ”overklig” eller svår att relatera till, vilket kan ses som ett hinder för att skapa en social kontakt liknande den som uppstår i ett vanligt kundmöte på apotek. För vissa väckte det osäkerhet inför vad roboten kunde förstå och hur den skulle agera, vilket tyder på att en bristande mänsklighet inte bara påverkar det emotionella intrycket utan även tilliten till robotens kommunikationsförmåga.

QP3.section: 8. Resultat > 1.3. Positiva visuella signaler i interaktionen > Tema 2: Språkliga egenskaper
QP3.text: Detta tema beskriver hur robotens språkliga egenskaper, såsom röst, språkbruk och språklig anpassning, påverkade deltagarnas upplevelse av tydlighet, förståelse och förtroende i kommunikationen.

QP4.text: I kapitlet beskrivs studiens metod, urval och deltagare, datainsamling och material samt analys av data. Studien baseras på intervjumaterial insamlat inom forskningsprojektet PharmAInteraction. I denna delstudie analyseras intervjuer med deltagare som interagerat med en social robot i en apotekskontext i laboratoriemiljö.

Denna studie har genomförts med en kvalitativ och beskrivande ansats, med syftet att fördjupa förståelsen för hur kunder upplever kommunikationen med en social robot i samband med läkemedelsrådgivning på apotek. En kvalitativ metod bedömdes som lämplig eftersom studien fokuserar på upplevelser, tolkningar och meningsskapande, snarare än på mätbara utfall eller generaliserbara samband (Graneheim & Lundman, 2004). Kvalitativ innehållsanalys med induktiv ansats enligt Graneheim och Lundman (2004) valdes för att möjliggöra en systematisk och transparent analys av intervjumaterialet. Metoden lämpar sig väl för att identifiera variationer i deltagarnas erfarenheter och för att synliggöra både manifesta och latenta innehåll i texten. Genom att arbeta stegvis med meningsbärande enheter, kondensering, kodning och kategorisering har analysen strävat efter att bevara deltagarnas perspektiv samtidigt som ett analytiskt djup har uppnåtts. En induktiv ansats valdes för att låta kategorier och teman växa fram ur materialet, snarare än att styras av förutbestämda teoretiska begrepp. Samtidigt har analysen genomförts med medvetenhet om studiens teoretiska ramverk, vilket innebär att tolkningen av resultaten senare relaterats till Jean Watsons Theory of Human Caring samt Halls teoretiska ramverk för tillit och förtroende. Detta kan ses som en kombination av induktiv analys och teoretisk tolkning i ett senare skede. Studien baseras på intervjuer som samlats in inom ramen för det större forskningsprojektet PharmAInteraction. Användningen av redan insamlat material kan ses som både en styrka och en begränsning. En styrka är att intervjuerna genomfördes i en kontrollerad och relevant kontext, med ett tydligt fokus på interaktion med en social robot i en simulerad apoteksmiljö.

QP4.section: 6. Material och metod > 6.1. Design och kontext
QP4.text: Studien är en delstudie inom forskningsprojektet PharmAInteraction, som genomförs vid Åbo Akademi i Vasa. Projektet undersöker hur sociala robotar kan stödja läkemedelsrådgivning på apotek. I denna delstudie analyseras redan insamlade intervjuer med personer som deltagit i rådgivningssituationer med den sociala roboten Furhat. Kontexten är en simulerad apoteksmiljö där roboten fungerade som rådgivare kring läkemedelsanvändning, med särskilt fokus på rådgivning om dagen efter piller. Studien har en kvalitativ och beskrivande design med syftet att öka förståelsen för hur människor upplever kommunikationen med en social robot under läkemedelsrådgivning. En kvalitativ ansats är lämplig när man vill fånga individers erfarenheter och upplevelser i sina egna ord (Graneheim & Lundman, 2004).

papers.title: Co-designing a social robot for child health care
papers.abstract: Social robots provide new opportunities to support general child healthcare programs. However, it is still unclear how social robots could be used in this context and how corresponding behaviors should be designed. To ensure satisfying implementations of such new technological solutions, it is essential to include the end-users in the designing process. We have conducted a co-design study at two primary schools based on three complementary, creative methods: Draw-write-and-tell and/or story-writing-and-telling, Theatre play, and Robot avatar programming. A total of 46 children aged 7 - 12 years old participated in four robot co-design workshops. The drawings, stories and theatre plays were analysed, resulting in evaluations of 10 scenarios as well as 21 new scenarios and 7 main user requirements for social robots providing mental support in general child healthcare. Evaluation of the activities highlight their stimulation of out-of-the-box thinking and the development of creative solutions (i.e. drawings/stories/theatre plays resulted in robot designs, scenarios and requirements), while children’s reflections show them being enjoyable for participation. The inputs gathered during these co-design workshops will greatly influence future work on the design and application of social robots in the child healthcare domain.

QP1.text: Also, personalization took place in multiple scenarios, for example ES3, where the robot would ask multiple questions to the child in order to adapt its behaviour to the child’s need, such as‘‘What kind of game would you like to play?’’. In multiple interactions, the social robot was a fun distraction, e.g., playing a game in the waiting room (ES5), explaining the vaccination in a fun and playful manner (ES4). In most plays, the robot expressed ‘robot-like’ behaviour (e.g., rigid movements) and speech (e.g., short factual sentences, monotonous voice). Table 4 Results of the children’s scenario evaluations. The requirements are further explained in Table 5. Child receives extra math lessons. To learn about this, the child takes a test with/on the robot. Child finds it difficult to talk about his feelings. How can the robot and care provider help? Child is shy and finds it difficult to play with other children. The robot finds this difficult too. How can they help each other? Child comes to the CJG for a vaccination. The child finds this a bit scary. There is a robot that explains the procedure. Child did very well on the assignment. Therefore, the child is allowed to choose a fun game to play with the robot. Child comes to the CJG for an eye test. Here the child has to wait. In the waiting area is a fun robot. The child comes to the CJG for the first time for a chat with the care provider. The child meets the care provider and the robot for the first time. The child feels a little shy.

Second, corresponding user requirements were derived from those scenarios and robot roles. Specifically, we were able to derive several requirements from the data, which could be grouped into 7 main user requirements including sub-requirements. A substantial part of our user requirement results further validate previous findings. The most important similarities are: the robot should be able to have a simple conversation with children (including asking questions Abubshait & Wiese, 2017; Breazeal, Kidd, Thomaz, Hoffman, & Berlin, 2005; Tung, 2016); the robot should have a humanoid (or zoomorphic) appearance (Beasley, 2012; Tung, 2016); the robots should be able to read and express emotions (Logan, Breazeal, Goodwin, Jeong, O’Connell, Smith-Freedman, Heathers, & Weinstock, 2019); and the robot should be able to act as a tutor or peer (Belpaeme et al., 2018; Mubin, Stevens, Shahid, Al Mahmud, & Dong, 2013). On top of these, we also identified additional requirements more specific to the child (mental) healthcare domain, such as the robot acting as a mediator in child-professionalparent interactions, and a robot helping in personalizing the treatment of the child. A final contribution of this paper are the method evaluations of the co-design activities used for the child healthcare domain. Children require special approaches and techniques as research participants. During the theatre activity, the children were less concentrated and wandered off the scenarios many times. This could perhaps be because the scenarios were a bit difficult for them to act out (depending on e.g., the age), or because their attention span was limited. These issues can be resolved by providing the children with more context in the scenarios, or by scheduling more breaks. However, the children still seemed very enthusiastic about the costumes and roles. By being flexible in adding or removing roles, letting the children think of plays themselves, asking the children whether they wanted to participate without forcing them, self-expression and creativity were stimulated. The children collaborated together surprisingly well, even with bigger age differences. The creativity involved in the activities seemed to make them suitable for every child in the broad age group of 7 to 12.

QP4.text: Therefore, in this paper, we present a human-centred co-design study aiming at designing and evaluating social robot behaviours for implementation in the general child healthcare domain, for and with children. Including end-users in the design of new technologies can increase usability and value of products (Norman, 2013). Children, depending on their age and development, can experience difficulties expressing themselves or may even be unaware of their own needs (Southam-Gerow & Kendall, 2002). Moreover, their attention span for active engagement is limited (Mahone & Schneider, 2012). It is therefore necessary to tailor co-design methods to children, allowing them to choose their own way of expressing and providing insights in their values, needs and situations (Darbyshire et al., 2005). The contribution of our paper consists of children’s evaluations of previously-derived social robot scenarios, as well as new scenarios and user requirements. Additionally, we evaluate different creative co-design methods, tailored to the needs of children.

In conclusion, children see potential in the use of social robots for child mental support in the general healthcare domain. Our participants came up with 21 new scenarios and, in addition, positively evaluated 9 scenarios created by adult end users (Neerincx, Rodenburg et al., 2021). These derived robot roles and user requirements serve as input for guidelines in designing social robot behaviours and applications for child mental support in the healthcare domain. Additionally, this paper provides in-depth insight into suitable methods and contexts for co-designing social robot interactions for child healthcare settings together with children. By providing the children with different ways of expressing themselves (see Table 1), our co-design methods resulted in new scenarios, scenario evaluations, robot roles, and user requirements for social robots in the child (mental) healthcare domain from the perspective of primary school children. The presented and evaluated co-design methods can already be used by other child–robot researcher in the community, while we are currently also developing followup design-test activities to further substantiate this set of co-design activities. Finally, our study provides further evidence for the suitability of a mixture of creative methods (i.e., drawing, writing, theatre play, programming) to involve children in the design of artificial intelligence technology such as social robots. Especially theatre play and programming is relevant for co-designing embodied agents such as social robots. Co-designing not only helps in designing for the user, it also helps in making the use and workings of technology such as social robots more transparent to the children themselves. The results of these co-design sessions will, together with previous research with involved adult users (e.g., child healthcare professionals, parents Neerincx, Rodenburg et al., 2021), contribute to designing low-risk applications of social robots in the child healthcare domain, which can then be tested in longterm, real-world settings (e.g., youth coaches at schools, social robots at vaccination days). The end goal is to design social robot interactions which are widely applicable.

QP4.section: 1. Introduction and related work > 1.2. Design space: Social robots in child healthcare
QP4.text: Child care professionals express the need for more long-term and specific research as well as concrete social robot applications for child mental support in healthcare settings (Neerincx, Rodenburg et al., 2021). The goal of our overall research project is to bridge this current gap of ecological validity and lacking knowledge of long-term effects by co-designing robot application scenarios with children, parents, and healthcare professionals, as well as systematically test these scenarios Table 1 An overview of the different creative co-design activities of the workshop. Story + at the Child and Family Center (individual). Drawing + and Family Center (individual). Play out one of the following 9 scenarios Video (or think of one yourself) (group). with longitudinal studies in real-world contexts. Child professionals are generally not familiar with existing social robot applications and their potential (Neerincx, Rodenburg et al., 2021; Rabbitt, Kazdin, & Scassellati, 2015), and neither are the children themselves. Yet, including the end users in the research and design process is essential to avoid non-adoption or rejection (De Graaf, Allouch, & Van Diik, 2017) and establish awareness of the potentials such robots may offer and identify the relevant user requirements (de Graaf, Ben Allouch, & van Dijk, 2018). A human-centred design approach can help in creating engaging child–robot interactions (Rose & Björling, 2017). The main users involved in our project are child healthcare professionals, parents and the children themselves. In previous work, we carried out focus groups with our adult end-users, which is an appropriate method for co-design purposes (Freitas, Oliveira, Jenkins, & Popjoy, 1998). However, children require other co-design methods given their inadequate capacities to express themselves and limited awareness of their own needs (Southam-Gerow & Kendall, 2002), and their narrow attention span for active engagement (Mahone & Schneider, 2012). Although children have been involved in co-design studies for technology, more specific co-design guidelines for social-robot interactions in general child care settings are still lacking.

papers.title: Social Robotics for Assessing Children’s Mental Wellbeing
papers.abstract: The rise in mental health and wellbeing concerns in children underscores the importance of developing solutions that are innovative, engaging and accessible. Traditional methods used for the evaluation of the mental wellbeing of individuals often do not capture wellbeing concerns in children, owing to limited resources, logistical limitations, stigma and most importantly, children’s restricted ability to articulate complex feelings. This thesis examines the use of Socially Assistive Robots (SARs) as a unique, non-intimidating and scalable approach for assessing the mental wellbeing of children, with an overarching focus on complementing current psychological frameworks to provide a more comprehensive overview of the wellbeing of children. This thesis is guided by three key lines of inquiry. Firstly, this work aims to investigate the feasibility of employing robot-led multimodal frameworks in administering mental wellbeing assessments for children 8-13 years of age, both in person in a physical, one-off interaction as well as online in a remote, longitudinal setting. By designing and deploying robot-led initiatives, this thesis demonstrates that the robot-assisted approaches are more effective in assessing wellbeing as compared to the traditional, existing methods. Further, we also observe that SARs have been successful in facilitating both one-off and repeated evaluations, thereby supporting both immediate as well as long-term assessment requirements. Secondly, this thesis also examines the integration of computational approaches that leverage verbal as well as non-verbal behaviour to provide a more holistic overview of the mental wellbeing of children. These methods enable more detailed and richer insights into the children’s emotional states and, as such, move beyond the self-reported measures of pediatric wellbeing that are currently used as established standards in the assessments. By leveraging data from multiple modalities such as audio, video and verbal responses, this thesis examines whether/how they can be used to inform automated assessments, thereby potentially aiding clinicians in making more informed decisions in relation to the wellbeing of children. Finally, this thesis also examines the children’s perception, validity as well as the disclosure implications of utilising robot-assisted frameworks in sensitive areas, such as the mental wellbeing domain, as these factors significantly impact their practical integration within real-world contexts. This line of inquiry addresses challenges related to examining user perceptions, validation of psychometrics for use in robot-led settings, and understanding the ethical nuances that govern robots’ role in cases where they become privy to information that might require support from the broader care network of children. Through empirical findings, computational modelling, and stakeholder discussions, this thesis aims to inform future mental wellbeing assessment tools using innovative and engaging SARs that carefully consider the nuances of emotion articulation in children. The principal goal is to provide valuable stepping stones towards developing frameworks that are accessible, innovative and ethically-informed for assessing the mental wellbeing of the future generation.

The rise in mental health and wellbeing concerns in children underscores the importance of developing solutions that are innovative, engaging and accessible. Traditional methods used for the evaluation of the mental wellbeing of individuals often do not capture wellbeing concerns in children, owing to limited resources, logistical limitations, stigma and most importantly, children’s restricted ability to articulate complex feelings. This thesis examines the use of Socially Assistive Robots (SARs) as a unique, non-intimidating and scalable approach for assessing the mental wellbeing of children, with an overarching focus on complementing current psychological frameworks to provide a more comprehensive overview of the wellbeing of children. This thesis is guided by three key lines of inquiry. Firstly, this work aims to investigate the feasibility of employing robot-led multi- modal frameworks in administering mental wellbeing assessments for children 8-13 years of age, both in person in a physical, one-o↵interaction as well as online in a remote, longitudinal setting. By designing and deploying robot-led initiatives, this thesis demonstrates that the robot-assisted approaches are more e↵ective in assessing wellbeing as compared to the traditional, existing methods. Further, we also observe that SARs have been successful in facilitating both one-o↵and repeated evaluations, thereby supporting both immediate as well as long-term assessment requirements. Secondly, this thesis also examines the integration of computational approaches that leverage verbal as well as non-verbal behaviour to provide a more holistic overview of the mental wellbeing of children. These methods enable more detailed and richer insights into the children’s emotional states and, as such, move beyond the self-reported measures of pediatric wellbeing that are currently used as established standards in the assessments. By leveraging data from multiple modalities such as audio, video and verbal responses, this thesis examines whether/how they can be used to inform automated assessments, thereby potentially aiding clinicians in making more informed decisions in relation to the wellbeing of children.

papers.title: Using Social Robots to Deliver Behaviour Change Interventions
papers.abstract: The acceleration of technology advancements has resulted in the growth of digital solutions to support with behaviour change in a wide range of domains. Social robots have been explored for their feasibility as agents to deliver established and novel talk-based person-centred behaviour change interventions, such as Motivational Interviewing and Functional Imagery Training (FIT), due to their interactive design and a way to support the growing pressures on health sectors. This thesis builds on previous feasibility work but explores the use of the social robots to support students in changing procrastination behaviours. There is a high prevalence of reported procrastination in students, despite the various consequences from increased stress and impact on mental health. The thesis initially explores the behaviours and domain of procrastination to support with the development of a FIT intervention that focuses on eliciting motivation to change behaviours while equipping people with imagery skills to maintain the motivation for change (Chapter 4). Chapter 5 includes two studies exploring social robots delivering FIT. Study one compared the differences in elicited behaviour change, motivation and confidence between a human therapist and robot delivering the same intervention over a four-week period. In the second study, to explore the importance of digital personalised talk-based therapy, a simple linear FIT intervention was compared to a more personalised approach. For both four-week trials, in addition to the change in motivation and procrastination, the therapeutic alliance formed was compared and the usability and intentions to use the robot in the future was measured. Due to the importance of eliciting change talk for successful behaviour change, the conversations between therapist and client were analysed for change and sustain talk to compare the effectiveness of the intervention and the mode of delivery (Chapter 6). This thesis also explores the perceptions of health professionals towards the use of social robots in the field of talk-based therapy after interacting with a social robot to support with future robot development and integration. To conclude, the current challenges faced with robot delivery and further research suggestions are made to ensure the future success of social robots as delivery agents for delivering behaviour change interventions.

QP1.section: 3 Digital Behaviour Change Interventions > Social robots as delivery agents of talk-based therapy > 3.2.2 Types of social robots
QP1.text: The final class of robots, with the highest level of complexity to their interactions are social robots. These robots pro-actively engage in a social manner to benefit the person, but also have their own internal goals and motivations. Social robots are equipped with the ability to mimic social traits within humans, including the use of gaze, making gestures, personalities, emotional expression and recognition, dialogue exchange, as well as the ability to understand and learn from others (Fong et al., 2003). These sociable robots have recently found purpose in a range of environments such as in hospitality (Nakanishi et al., 2020), entertainment (Lytridis et al., 2019), therapy and health care (Cifuentes et al., 2020), rehabilitation (Céspedes et al., 2021) and educational settings (Ahmad et al., 2020). Over recent years, social robots have developed and vary in their complexity of communication and their modalities of communication. The Nao robot, developed by Softbank Robotics (Softbank Robotics, 2018) is a popular social robot with a humanoid presence. Nao robots have commonly been used in research and education (Amirova et al., 2021). The Nao robot is equipped with motors to allow it to move and adapt to its environment, touch sensors for people to interact with and to use to locate itself in space, microphones and speakers for verbal interaction, cameras that allow for object and person recognition and also speech recognition and dialogue in multiple languages. A more advanced humanoid robot is the Pepper robot, also developed by Softbank Robotics (Softbank Robotics, 2021). Pepper has similar features to Nao but has advances in its abilities to move and interact with humans. It makes use of a touch screen on its chest to display content and support interaction with humans. Furhat (Furhat Robotics, 2021) is an advanced social robot that takes the form of a human head that displays a multitude of digital faces onto a physical mask. This allows the projection of human faces, to animation and animals. It uses life-like expressiveness to mimic human behaviour and the automatic face movements give illusion of life, including having advanced computer tracking from face tracking and ability to assess engagement.

QP1.section: 3 Digital Behaviour Change Interventions > Social robots as delivery agents of talk-based therapy > 3.2.2 Types of social robots
QP1.text: Although social robots all have the aim of engaging with humans they have been categorised into subclasses based on their varying capabilities and levels of complex interaction they can achieve to participate in interactions and communicate with humans (Breazeal, 2003). In all subclasses, humans tend of make sense of the complex behaviour by anthropomorphising the robots and the interactions they have with them. Examples of this subclass include Paro (Wada et al., 2006), a robotic seal that uses a variety of complex sensors to interact and learn from its user, but its interaction is limited to movement and sounds to reflect a real seal. Social interface robots use human-like social cues to facilitate their interactions with people, including gaze, gestures, and facial expression to convey a message. They can be used as a physical counterpart for distal humans. However, the interaction with this type of robot is usually shallow with a simple social complexity model. Socially receptive robots are more complex in their human interactions, and the robots themselves also benefit from the interactions, such as learning from a human demonstration and affect the robot’s internal structure at a deeper level. They are a socially passive class of robot as they do not pro-actively engage with people to fulfil social aims, however they are able to perceive social cues allowing humans to guide and shape the robot’s behaviour.

QP1.section: 3 Digital Behaviour Change Interventions > Social robots as delivery agents of talk-based therapy
QP1.text: Social robots combine the advantages of chatbots with a device that offers a physical embodied presence, potentially enhancing the scope for the development of a strong working alliance between client and the digital therapist. The following section will introduce social robots, discuss their areas of application and why they potentially suited agents for delivery of talk-based therapy. A robot is a programmable machine which is able to complete a task without human interference. These tasks are traditionally monotonous or considered of high risk and work separately from humans. They have served a range of purposes in different applications such as within industry, agriculture, construction (Siciliano & Khatib, 2016)). However, with the progression in robotics, there are growing use cases for them to work alongside and interact with humans. Social robots are designed to interact within a human environment and communicate in an interpersonal manner. This level of communication with robots is designed to create a human-robot interaction, with the robot seen as a partner to achieve positive outcomes. Although social robots commonly take a humanoid or animal-like form, this does not have to be the case as long as they are communicating and coordinating their behaviour effectively with humans (Breazeal et al., 2016). The robots are designed to communicate via verbal, non-verbal or affective modalities to allow them to actively engage in human communication and behaviours.

QP2.text: Further, although done to avoid breaking down the flow of conversation as experienced in Kanaoka and Mutlu (2015), the pressing of the sensors to move on the conversation does not offer the same natural flow of conversation that can be experienced with a human. Therefore, future robot delivery would also need to be aware of natural conversational timings to ensure users are not interrupted mid intervention. Despite what may be considered barriers for the robot at this stage, the simple branching approach taken in this study did still result in the robot successfully eliciting all categories of change talk. Despite the simplicity of the programming of the social robot used in this study, it is important to highlight that even without the full presence and natural use of the OARS within the intervention, the social robot still elicited all types of change talk. The social robot was unable to offer open questions or offer summaries directly related to the content the participants were providing, and affirmations were only loosely connected to the feedback. The FIT scripts focused on the participant creating their own reflections and only offering simple tailored ones within the branched experience, however even this simple level of MI and FIT features elicited change talk. This is in line with Apodaca et al. (2016) who found even simple reflections from therapists would elicit change talk and support with ambivalence. This would suggest that individuals did progress through the stages of change outlined in the Transtheoretical Model (J. O. Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983) due to the change talk present within the interventions, despite the simplistic delivery of the intervention. It may be that as technology advances, robots are able to identify the key phrases within change talk statements that signify when an individual has progressed onto the next stage of change and therefore offer a more natural experience of intervention delivery.

QP2.section: Methods > 5.4.2 Materials > 5.4.2.1 Mode of delivery and Robot coding
QP2.text: Figure 3: Screen taken from Choregraphe window to demonstrate coding taken place to develop the intervention into the Nao Robot. Nao was designed to work autonomously without the facilitation of a researcher in the room. The voice parameters were sets to 100%, with the voice adjusted to a speed of 80% for intervention delivery. The robot was coded with a soft breathing motion built into the Choregraphe software to give the robot a sense of realistic movement and attentiveness and used gestures at relevant points of the intervention. The face tracking feature was used to allow the robots gaze to follow the participants to offer the simulation of the robot being attentive to the individual and signally that it is listening. The sensors within the robot were utilised to facilitate the turn-taking during the conversation. This was to limit the technical complications faced in previous research (Kanaoka & Mutlu, 2015) where the fluency of the conversation between human and robot interrupted the formation of collaboration between human. This was due to the speech recognition not being reliable enough in capturing, interpreting, and responding to responses. The tactile sensors within the feet and head of the Nao robot were programmed for the user to respond to questions and document their answers or to progress the conversation. To further encourage the turn taking, the robot’s eyes were programmed to change from blue to green when the robot was in “listening mode” to encourage the user to speak. At times, during the branched-robot condition, the responses to the robot were documented and the robot would respond accordingly to changes in confidence over time, or choices made to offer a level of personalisation, such as when choosing topic areas to discuss. The same robot and coding process was used to deliver the booster video sessions at the one-week point of the trial. The robot was coded, with videos recorded of the sessions to be build into an online platform for participants to access from home, to facilitate boosters fitting into daily routines.

Despite the importance of eliciting change-talk, very few digitally delivered interventions require the individual to voice out loud their thoughts, goals, and actions. To encourage interaction with the interventions to cement goals, previous interventions have employed various approaches. One approach being the “Wizard of Oz” concept, whereby computers give the illusion they are providing personalised responses to users but instead a human is in control of the programme behind the screen. Kahler et al. (2017) adopted this approach due to the limited capacity of AI speech recognition. Although the benefits to this concept were demonstrated to facilitate text-based conversation, the approach does not provide a long-term sustainable solution to digital delivery. Beyond typing, speaking aloud directly to technology has received limited attention. Social robots have been employed as agents to deliver interventions due to them offering a humanoid presence to an intervention, which have been designed with the intent to interact with people through verbal and non- verbal communication to facilitate a human-robot interaction (Bartneck et al., 2020). However, the technology is still restricted with its speech recognition ability. Kanaoka and Mutlu, (2015) used a Nao robot to deliver an MI script where participants could freely respond, but the technology constraints resulted in disruptions to the participants illusions and broke the collaboration needed for MI. Therefore, more recent work has focused on robots not responding directly to participants comments and instead focused on programming responses that work regardless of the comment. This approach allowed participants to still voice aloud their goals and plans to reach them to elicit motivation but avoided the constraints of speech recognition (Galvão Gomes da Silva et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2020b). Participants expressed acceptance to the robot delivery, commenting on the novelty of the technology making it memorable but that the ability to hear their goals aloud was motivating (Galvão Gomes da Silva et al., 2018; Robinson et al., 2020b).

QP3.section: Results > 7.3.2 Qualitative responses > 7.3.2.4 Robot vs Human > Design recommendations for social robots delivering talk-based therapies
QP3.text: Insights gathered from the health professionals within this study offer suggestion to the direction social robot talk-based therapy should take, offering recommendations for design and implementation of such technology. The focus of the recommendations were around the interaction between the robot and client to ensure successful delivery of the talk-based therapies, rather than the robots appearance. After interacting with the robot, or receiving a demonstration, the professionals highlighted the importance in the need to improve the conversational skills of the robot for successful delivery. Although benefits were raised despite the limited conversational skills of the Nao robot demonstrated, specific attention was given to the need for the robot to be able to understand what the client was saying. It was suggested that this would support the development of a fluent conversation to encourage more interaction between the robot and client and further develop the alliance. Further, future development should focus on the robot personality to ensure it is approachable and supportive and replicate one of a therapist. The robot having a realistic appearance was not seen as important, nor was the voice or body language of the robot or at least not until the conversational ability of the robot has been addressed. It was highlighted that the robot did offer a non-judgemental environment but the ability to both detect, and express emotions was raised by professionals to be an important future consideration. Future robot delivery needs to be able to detect the emotions of clients and respond appropriately, as well as having reactive emotions to these both physically and verbally. The ability for the robot to express emotion would encourage understanding and empathy, as displayed in human delivery.

Unlike previous studies analysing change talk (Galvão Gomes da Silva et al., 2020, Nurmi, 2020), this study compared the same content delivered by two different agents to assess whether a human would elicit more change talk regardless of the content delivered. One area that humans are able to deliver more effectively than robots is empathy due to the robot not having the ability to understand and experience the feelings of another. Expressing empathy is considered a core component of MI and MI-based interventions and is necessary for successful exploration of change and linked to positive treatment outcomes (Miller & Rollnick, 1991, 2002; Moyers & Miller, 2013). Clinician empathy speech has also been positively correlated with the level of client change talk (Fischer & Moyers, 2014). Due to the limitations of the robot speech recognition, the branched script used did not allow for high levels of empathy to be present. Although recordings allowed for monitoring of the human delivery to ensure the branched script was adhered to, the human agent is able to express empathy through body language, facial expressions and offer vocal confirmation to demonstrate to the participant they are listening. Further, humans are naturally inclined to disclose more to humans, as well as the disclosure being richer and longer in comparison to robots (Laban et al., 2021). Although the robot was coded to offer movement, it is unable to offer these communicative behaviours that may support in encouraging comfort to discuss answers. Despite this, the robot elicited higher levels of change talk in both conditions.

Further, although done to avoid breaking down the flow of conversation as experienced in Kanaoka and Mutlu (2015), the pressing of the sensors to move on the conversation does not offer the same natural flow of conversation that can be experienced with a human. Therefore, future robot delivery would also need to be aware of natural conversational timings to ensure users are not interrupted mid intervention. Despite what may be considered barriers for the robot at this stage, the simple branching approach taken in this study did still result in the robot successfully eliciting all categories of change talk. Despite the simplicity of the programming of the social robot used in this study, it is important to highlight that even without the full presence and natural use of the OARS within the intervention, the social robot still elicited all types of change talk. The social robot was unable to offer open questions or offer summaries directly related to the content the participants were providing, and affirmations were only loosely connected to the feedback. The FIT scripts focused on the participant creating their own reflections and only offering simple tailored ones within the branched experience, however even this simple level of MI and FIT features elicited change talk. This is in line with Apodaca et al. (2016) who found even simple reflections from therapists would elicit change talk and support with ambivalence. This would suggest that individuals did progress through the stages of change outlined in the Transtheoretical Model (J. O. Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983) due to the change talk present within the interventions, despite the simplistic delivery of the intervention. It may be that as technology advances, robots are able to identify the key phrases within change talk statements that signify when an individual has progressed onto the next stage of change and therefore offer a more natural experience of intervention delivery.

QP4.section: Methods > 5.8.2 Materials > 5.8.2.5 Robot Incentives, Self-Efficacy and Usage Intentions Scales
QP4.text: The Robot Incentives Scale (RIS), The Robot Self-Efficacy Scale (RSES) and the Usage Intention (Robinson et al., 2018) were used to measure incentives to interact with a social robot, confidence to interact with a social robot and intentions to use social robots. The RIS is a 11-item scale measured on a 0-10 scale, from “not at all” to “definitely” with three subscales: ‘emotion’, ‘social’ and ‘utility’. ‘Emotion’ measured the likeability of the robot, ‘social’ assessed the perceived sociability and ‘utility’ for the perceived utility of the robot. The RSES is another 11-iem scale to measure how confident users are in interacting with the robot and has two sub-sections: operation of the robot and the application of applying it to a task. The scale is measured on a 0 – 10 scale, from “sure I can’t” to “sure I can”. Usage intention of the robot is a short 5-item scale, with a 0-10 scale ranging from “not at all” to

Attendees were free to interact with the robot for as long as they wished, but the demonstration would last 5-10 minutes depending on whether they fully role-played the interaction by responding to the questions. Further to the demonstration stand, the lead researcher (LC) held a workshop session which comprised of a short 25-minute talk discussing the potential of social robots to support healthcare, exploring initial results from research in the field and discussing future steps. As part of the workshop, the robot was also demonstrated to attendees and a question-and-answer session was held. At the end of the interaction at either the demonstration stands or the workshop, attendees were invited to answer the short online questionnaire to document their perceptions towards the robot after having seen the robot in action. Perceptions were collected via a survey due to the convenience of capturing thoughts from professionals while attending a conference, and the challenges of recruiting and organising qualitative methods during an event. The survey was a mix of open and closed questions to explore the perceptions of the conference attendees around the use of social robots, contents of questionnaire available in Table 8 (the full survey is available in Appendix D). Table 8: Contents of questionnaire used to explore health professionals’ perceptions of the social robot presented at the conference.

Participants perceptions were explored further through open-ended questions to understand their potential advantages, barriers, and features to make the robot more effective. As a result of thematic analysis conducted on the 76 responses received to the open-ended questions, four main themes emerged: breadth, delivery, practicality, and robot vs. human. Themes and codes are presented in Table 10. Table 10: Codes and themes produced from thematic analysis conducted on open-ended questions.

papers.title: New Friends: Social Robots in Therapy and Education

QP1.text: Another challenge related to usage in real life is the acceptance of personal robots in the home. Jochum et al. described an innovative approach to inﬂuence the acceptance of care robots using theatrical performance. They investigated how audiences perceive social robots interacting with humans in a future care scenario through a scripted performance. In the subsequent contribution, Özcan et al. investigate the issue of suitable robot forms for particular therapeutic domains. They present a novel concept of interactive devices, called ‘transitional wearable companions’: soft interactive animal shaped devices, able to evoke emotions and giving a continuous reassuring physical contact. Their application is to support therapy and foster social skill development in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), giving a therapist a range of possibilities with in- and output control, and gather biosensor information on the child’s physiological and emotional state. A contribution by Looije et al. reports on a study of how social robots can be used to support the development of selfmanagement of children with diabetes. They develop proﬁles for further personalization of such a robot, and describe general requirements for mediating the support of parents and caregivers. Finally, a study by Scholten et al. addresses the application of hygiene protocols in a clinical environment and establishes to what extend such protocols can be applied to robotic animals that are currently used in this setting. Their paper features essential principles to be observed by researchers in this ﬁeld and presents a framework for further research. The next two contributions address design issues of socially interactive robots to be applied in different kinds of therapy. Issues include affect and embodiment.

De Beir et al. address the design of affective expressive capabilitiesofsocialrobotsintheformofeyebrowsonaNAO robot (that does not have eyebrows by default). They present a technically clever solution to add eyebrows as a module to the NAO and show in a user study that the expressions of sadness versus happiness are reliably recognized even when the robot performs gestures at the same time (they test two different gestures). Canamero et al. present the design of a cognitively and motivationally autonomous affective robot toddler. It has been developed to support perceived self-efﬁcacy and emotional wellbeing in children with diabetes, applying an ‘Embodied AI’ approach, which is argued to fulﬁll the therapeutic and affective requirements of the target group beyond other approaches commonly used in assistive robotics and child-robot interaction. Finally, ﬁvepapers focus onthetechnical, ethical andsocietal landscape needed for therapeutic and educational use of social robots. Reppou et al. propose a software architecture that facilitates deployment and ﬂexible addition of functionality to smart home systems, including robots. They propose a cloudbased solution that facilitates the development of novel apps, together with ofﬂine machine learning modules as well as databases that learn and store user data. Of course they pay extra attention to data privacy, for example, in the way Robot apps are deployed in the system. A study by Zubrycki et al. presents a project named Roboterapia. This project concerns an environment supporting the needs of therapists working with children with special developmental needs, developed and tested in the ﬁeld of autism treatment. The authors report on the developmental process, eliciting and specifying the needs of therapists and the produced prototype devices that could support different aspects of therapists’ work.

New Friends: Social Robots in Therapy and Education Marcel Heerink1 · Bram Vanderborght2 · Joost Broekens3 · Jordi Albó-Canals4 Published online: 25 August 2016 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2016 This special issue reﬂects this multidisciplinary ﬁeld of social robots in therapy and education with a broad collection of contributions, concerning technical, therapeutic, educational and ethical issues. The application of social robots in therapy and education is an emerging ﬁeld. This development is fueled by the fact that these ‘new friends’ become more sophisticated, available and affordable. In recent years there has been an enormous increase of projects in which social robots are used successfully for groups with special needs, such as people with dementia, hospitalized children and children with autism. These projects demand expertise from a wide range of disciplines, like psychology, nursing, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, AI, robotics and education to meet the technical opportunities with the development of therapeutic and educational practice. The ﬁrst ﬁve papers are addressing usage and relevant methodological issues concerning the use in therapy or edu- m.heerink@windesheimﬂevoland.nl Bram Vanderborght bram.vanderborght@vub.ac.be Robotics Research Group, Windesheim University, Almere, The Netherlands Brussels Human Centered Robotic research center (BruBotics), Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Brussels, Belgium Intelligent Systems, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands Engineering School, La Salle - Ramon Llull University, Barcelona, Spain cation of either a speciﬁc social robot, a speciﬁc category of social robots or social robots in general. A ﬁrst well-known application ﬁeld of socially assistive robots is autism. As technology becomes increasingly integrated into daily life, understanding how the cognitive capabilities of social robots impact human WB has become crucial. Figure 6 illustrates the Likert scale responses reflecting perceptions of the cognitive abilities of social robots across four statements. The interaction system utilized in this study involved AI-powered social robots equipped with advanced emotional recognition capabilities. Each robot was designed to engage in verbal and non-verbal communication, including EI and adaptive learning. The recording system consisted of high-definition cameras and microphones to capture both the visual and audio aspects of the interaction. Additionally, physiological data (e.g., heart rate) was monitored during the sessions to assess emotional responses. Participants interacted with the robot for 20-min sessions, conducted in a controlled laboratory environment. The robots’ responses were customized based on real-time analysis of the participant’s emotional state, adapting to the context of the conversation and engagement.

QP4.text: In this study, the cognitive skills of social robots are operationally defined as their proficiency in tasks that necessitate problem-solving skills, the capacity for learning and adaptation, and the quality of interactions with humans. In a social environment, these skills are important for assessing how effectively robots can understand and respond to human needs in real-time situations, making them important indicators of robot competence. Measurement Tools In this study, the primary data collection tool was a structured questionnaire incorporating a 5-point Likert scale. This scale allows participants to express their agreement or disagreement with the statements regarding social robots’ cognitive abilities on a continuum ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Likert scales of this nature are widely employed in research for the ability to capture nuanced responses and quantify participants’ attitudes and perceptions effectively.

The questionnaire was developed with careful consideration of relevant literature, drawing from existing frameworks and scales to accurately assess participants’ emotional states and attitudes towards social robots (refer to Appendix Table 8 for the questionnaire). Specifically, the authors referenced studies like Kim and Mutlu (2014), which explored how social distance influences human–robot interaction, and Ninomiya et al. (2015), who developed the Multi-Dimensional Robot Attitude Scale to evaluate people’s attitudes toward domestic robots. Additionally, the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-42) by Ab Aziz and Jemili (2022), which is widely used to measure mental health indicators such as depression, anxiety, and stress, was incorporated to assess the participants’ emotional WB and psychological needs. These foundational sources informed the design of the survey, ensuring that it captured a broad spectrum of emotional states and attitudes about robot interactions. The integration of these established psychological scales helped the authors create a comprehensive tool for measuring shifts in emotional states before and after robot interactions. The final survey was distributed to 1,000 participants, with 961 completed responses, achieving a 90.01% response rate and ensuring a robust and reliable dataset for analysis. This extensive sample size enhances the generalizability of the findings, offering valuable insights into the effects of social robots on human emotions and WB. To ensure a diverse and representative sample, participants were recruited through online platforms, including social media, university mailing lists, and research networks. This approach allowed for broad geographical representation across various regions of China. Efforts were made to include individuals from different age groups, genders, educational backgrounds, and urban/rural locations. The high response rate was achieved through strategies such as providing a user-friendly survey, sending timely reminders, offering incentives like entry into a prize draw, and ensuring the confidentiality of responses. These combined efforts contributed to a strong and reliable dataset for the study.

To complement the quantitative data, semi-structured interviews are conducted to obtain deeper qualitative insights. These interviews explore participants’ perceptions and experiences with the social robots, focusing particularly on how the cognitive abilities of these robots align with and fulfill the participants’ needs. By employing open-ended questions, the interviews allow for an in-depth exploration of individual experiences, capturing nuances that structured data collection methods might miss. This qualitative component is crucial for understanding the complex dynamics between human emotional states and robot interactions in real-world settings. The study combined both qualitative and quantitative methods to explore the impact of social robots’ cognitive abilities on human WB. The theoretical framework was grounded in human–robot interaction literature, focusing on EI, anxiety, and user satisfaction. This framework guided the design of both qualitative and quantitative data collection methods, ensuring comprehensive insights into the relationship between emotional states and social robot interactions. In-depth interviews were conducted with participants exhibiting varying levels of anxiety, aiming to understand their emotional needs and preferences regarding social robots. Semi-structured interviews allowed flexibility in exploring individual perspectives, and participants were selected based on their mental WB status to ensure diverse viewpoints. Thematic analysis was employed to identify recurring patterns in participants’ experiences with social robots. A structured survey was distributed to a larger sample to quantify participants’ anxiety levels and user satisfaction with social robots. The survey included validated scales to assess anxiety and satisfaction, with participants rating their experiences on a Likert scale. The sample was representative of individuals from various age groups and backgrounds, ensuring the generalizability of the findings. This quantitative data complemented the qualitative insights by providing statistical evidence of the relationship between emotional states, cognitive abilities of robots, and user satisfaction.

papers.title: Exploring the Use of Social Robots for Depression Screening Among Older Adults: An Expanded Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Depression in older adults affects health and can increase suicide risk, so early detection and timely referral matter. The objective of this study was to assess feasibility of social robot (SR) administration of the GDS-15 by comparing decision-relevant screening outcomes with a healthcare professional (HP), comparing embodied and avatar SR modalities, and evaluating affect (PANAS) and robot perceptions (Godspeed). Building on a 5-participant pilot suggesting comparable triage-level classifications, we ran a counterbalanced within-participant study with 20 older adults (10 SR first, 10 HP first; 10 embodied, 10 avatar). We mapped GDS-15 scores to screening outcomes (0–5 vs 6–15; unlikely, possible, likely) and quantified agreement with percent agreement, Cohen’s kappa (weighted for ordinal), and McNemar’s exact test. Using HP as an operational reference, we computed sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy, and absolute SR–HP score deviations in GDS-15 points. Score-level method-comparison summaries included ICC(A,1) and Bland-Altman bias and limits of agreement. A paired TOST equivalence test supported equivalence of the mean SR–HP score difference for Δ = 2 points, with sensitivity analyses for Δ = 1 and Δ = 1.5 points. Exploratory order-effect and cognitive-status sensitivity analyses did not materially change agreement estimates in this sample. PANAS showed no adverse affect impact during SR-administered screening, and Godspeed responses were positive. These findings support social robots as a supervised interface for GDS-15 administration and decision-relevant screening outcomes in this cohort. papers.title: Toward Personalized Social Robots for Child Well-being: Data Requirement Principles from a Recommender-System Perspective
papers.abstract: Social robots are increasingly deployed in clinical settings to support the well-being of children, where effective support must be personalized to each child. Personalization, choosing the robot action best suited to each child, can be framed as a recommendation problem, and a recently proposed recommender-system framework for social robots offers a principled approach through user profiling, ranking, and responsible computing. Instantiating it, however, is blocked not by the model but by the data, which is hard to gather. A child's state shifts within and across visits, so no fixed description of the user holds. Within a session, the few signals of whether the robot's actions helped are weak and indirect. Across sessions, children are rarely seen more than once, and anonymization breaks the identity needed to link visits. Because care cannot be randomized, existing data is observational, biased toward whatever was already done. Each is a familiar recommender-system problem, and we propose four data principles in response: an integrated profile, effectiveness signals, linkable coverage, and an exposure record logged at collection time. We identify which of these principles each capability requires, and frame them as concrete guidelines for data collection.

QP1.section: I. INTRODUCTION > Fine-grained, identity-linked, action-level data
QP1.text: Existing vs. required data collection for personalized social robots in child well-being settings. Left: existing robot-administered assessments reduce a session to a single anonymized score, which can neither build a user profile nor link to one. Right: the proposed collection logs one record per robot action, holding the child’s state (P1), the action and the reaction that follows (P2), and why the action was chosen (P4), all tied to a linkable identity across visits and children (P3) into an integrated profile that recommender-system models can learn from. P1–P4 refer to the four data principles of Section IV. The robot depicted is the social robot Haru [1]. develops them, examines how far existing data meets them, and identifies which principles each capability requires.

Accepted as a Late Breaking Report (LBR) at IEEE RO-MAN 2026 Toward Personalized Social Robots for Child Well-being: Data Requirement Principles from a Recommender-System Perspective Jin Huang1,∗, Eric Nichols2,∗, Fethiye Irmak Do˘gan1, and Hatice Gunes1 Abstract— Social robots are increasingly deployed in clinical settings to support the well-being of children, where effective support must be personalized to each child. Personalization, choosing the robot action best suited to each child, can be framed as a recommendation problem, and a recently proposed recommender-system framework for social robots offers a principled approach through user profiling, ranking, and responsible computing. Instantiating it, however, is blocked not by the model but by the data, which is hard to gather. A child’s state shifts within and across visits, so no fixed description of the user holds. Within a session, the few signals of whether the robot’s actions helped are weak and indirect. Across sessions, children are rarely seen more than once, and anonymization breaks the identity needed to link visits. Because care cannot be randomized, existing data is observational, biased toward whatever was already done. Each is a familiar recommendersystem problem, and we propose four data principles in response: an integrated profile, effectiveness signals, linkable coverage, and an exposure record logged at collection time. We identify which of these principles each capability requires, and frame them as concrete guidelines for data collection.

This need is concrete in real-world applications. For instance, at Hospital Virgen del Rocío in Seville, Spain, the social robot Haru [1] provides companionship and conducts anxiety screening for children undergoing cancer treatment [7]. Many of these children, such as those with leukemia, return repeatedly over months of care, and their anxiety, understanding, and emotional state differ from one child to the next and shift from visit to visit. To effectively support them, the robot must adapt both to the individual child and to how that child changes over time. Personalization is, therefore, the capability these applications require. Yet the data needed to learn it is hard to gather. We identify four challenges: (i) A child’s anxiety, attention, and understanding shift within and across visits, so no fixed description of the user holds [8]. (ii) Within a session, children typically give few direct signals of whether the interaction helped, often at its conclusion, and the rest must be inferred from weak, indirect cues [9]. (iii) Across sessions, most children are seen only once while a few return repeatedly, and consent and anonymization break the per-child identity that linking visits depends on, so a usable cross-session history rarely exists [10], [11]. (iv) Because care cannot be randomized, existing data is observational, biased toward whatever was already done [12]. These are not limitations of scale: collecting more data under the same designs would not yield what personalization requires; the data must be designed, not merely accumulated. None of these challenges is new. Each is a problem recommender systems are built to handle: a non-stationary user state (i), implicit feedback (ii), cold-start and unlinkable histories (iii), and off-policy bias (iv). Building on a recent recommender-system framework for social robots [13], we argue that what stands between that framework and these applications is not the model but the data it can learn from.

QP2.text: Ensuring the well-being of children is a priority shared by parents, educators, and clinicians, and it depends not only on a child’s physical care but on how the people around them respond to their needs. This is most acute in clinical settings, where illness and medical procedures place children under stress. Social robots are increasingly brought in to offer companionship and emotional reassurance, and to help children understand what is happening to them [2]– [4]. However, children vary widely in developmental stage, anxiety, prior knowledge, and language, so effective support must be personalized to each child [5], [6]. ∗These authors contributed equally and are co-first authors. 1J. A. Social robots and data collection in hospital settings Social robots are increasingly deployed in hospitals and clinics for patient-facing roles, including companionship and emotional support [2], patient education and explanation [21], screening and assessment [14], [16], [19], [22], procedural distraction [5], [6], and longer-term selfmanagement and monitoring [17], [23], across adult and pediatric populations and platforms such as NAO, Pepper, Furhat, and Haru [7], [24]. Our concern here is less the breadth of these applications than how they collect data. As Table I illustrates, user data comes predominantly from robot-administered standardized instruments and patientreported outcome measures [14]–[16]; interaction is typically rule-based or scripted, with large language models only recently introduced [20], [25]; and study designs are mostly single-session, recording outcomes as end-of-session scores and user-experience ratings [10].

QP3.section: II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK > B. Review of RS-inspired framework for social robots
QP3.text: We build on the framework of [13], which reframes personalization in social robots as a recommendation problem and integrates three modular, plug-and-play components into the robot’s cognition pipeline. User profiling models a user’s preferences at complementary granularities: longterm interests via collaborative filtering, short-term intent via sequential modeling, and fine-grained preferences via knowledge-enhanced modeling. Ranking scores and orders candidate robot actions for the current user and selects the most appropriate one to execute. Responsible computing constrains these operations to preserve privacy, mitigate bias, and promote fairness. Instantiating these components in the clinical child well-being setting presupposes data of a particular kind (e.g., data linking each user’s profile and state to the robot actions they receive and the responses these elicit); whether it is available in existing datasets or under current data-collection strategies is an open question. QP3.section: III. HOW EXISTING DATA MEETS PERSONALIZATION
QP3.text: Patient-facing social-robot studies, such as those in Table I, are built to screen or assess a single construct: the robot administers a standardized instrument, and what the session yields is a single score summarizing the user’s state on that construct. Personalization needs data of a different kind, a record of how each user responded to what the robot did, linked to that user’s state and accumulated across many users. Against this record, existing data falls short on each of the four challenges of Section I. Across these studies, the user is described and recorded through the instrument administered and the single construct it measures, one description per session. The description is fixed in two senses: fixed in advance to the one dimension the instrument targets, although what shifts in the child spans several dimensions at once; and fixed over the interaction, although that shifting state is what the robot’s actions must adapt to (Challenge i). Feedback takes the form of a questionnaire given once the session is over, a rating of how satisfied the user was with the interaction or the robot overall. It reports whether the session as a whole landed well, but not which of the robot’s actions within it the user responded to and which they did not, so the per-action signal a preference model would be trained and evaluated on is absent (Challenge ii). Most children are seen only once, and consent and anonymization strip the per-child identity that ties one visit to the next, so a child’s sessions cannot be assembled into a history. The per-user history that personalizing to a returning child would build on therefore does not exist (Challenge iii). This last challenge is not a shortfall of the existing studies: with only a few conditions to compare, collection can randomize over them and stay unbiased. The per-action preferences personalization needs, however, range over an action space too large to randomize over, so the data is observational, biased toward whatever was already done (Challenge iv).

This section introduces the requirements of data that suit the RS framework as four principles, one per challenge: an integrated profile (Challenge i), effectiveness signals (Challenge ii), linkable, representative coverage (Challenge iii), and an exposure record (Challenge iv). Principle 1 (Integrated profile). The data should record each user’s dimensions jointly as a single multi-layer profile (identity, dynamic emotional state, interaction history, situational context, and multimodal signals), rather than as isolated attributes. Existing datasets each model a single construct, because they are built for screening or assessment rather than for personalizing actions, so few datasets hold these dimensions together for the same user. Yet what action suits a user depends on their combination, not on any attribute alone. Unless the dimensions are recorded jointly, this combination is never observed, and personalization can respond to only one factor at a time. For example, a child returning for treatment over months may arrive anxious, yet already familiar with the procedure ahead. Anxiety alone cannot determine the action: comforting and explaining are both reasonable responses to an anxious child. Her familiarity is what decides: since she already knows what will happen, explaining would not help her anxiety, and the robot should comfort her instead. Principle 2 (Effectiveness signals). The data should align each robot action, identified by its content rather than as an opaque item, with the user behavior that follows it, both explicit behavior (follow-up questions, requests to rephrase, a brief per-action rating) and implicit signals (hesitations, gaze, facial expression), so that fine-grained preference for individual actions can be inferred and generalized to new ones.
